results.title: JarvisLabs GPU 怎么选？L4、A100、H100、H200 价格与暂停计费 | 智机玄同
results.author: 智机玄同 发布于 2026年10月10日 3 分钟阅读
highlights:
JarvisLabs 提供按分钟 GPU VM、Templates、Serverless 与 Clusters。本文核对 2026 年 10 月新价格和暂停后的存储费用。

智机玄同发布于 2026年10月10日 3 分钟阅读

资料核查日期： 2026年10月10日。价格、库存和服务商规则可能变化，请以官方页面为准。

文章目录

2026 年 9 月 24 日，JarvisLabs 发布了一条容易漏看的价格更新。

H100 SXM、H200 SXM 和 RTX PRO 6000 的 On-Demand 新价格从 10 月 5 日生效。旧价格仍能出现在部分页面摘要里，但已经不适合当作当前新实例报价。

本站按生效日期使用新价，并把 Reserved 与 Spot 留在普通 Compare 之外。

## 四种运行方式

JarvisLabs 当前提供 On-Demand GPU VM、预装环境 Templates、Serverless 和 GPU Clusters。

VM 给完整 root 权限。Templates 更适合直接打开 JupyterLab、VS Code 或 SSH。Serverless 面向模型端点。Clusters 则服务更大的多节点任务。

同一张 GPU 在不同产品里的交付方式不同。本文的结构化报价只记录单 GPU On-Demand VM。

## 当前单 GPU On-Demand 价格

截至 2026-10-10，面向印度以外客户的公开 USD 价格如下。

| GPU | vCPU | RAM | USD / GPU 小时 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| L4 24GB | 32 | 124GB | 0.44 |
| A100 80GB SXM | 16 | 112GB | 1.49 |
| RTX PRO 6000 Server Edition 96GB | 28 | 160GB | 2.19 |
| H100 SXM 80GB | 16 | 200GB | 3.49 |
| H200 SXM 141GB | 28 | 300GB | 4.59 |

价格按 GPU 小时展示，实例按分钟计费。

A100 40GB 仍有公开小时价，但官方当前租赁配置没有清楚标明本站需要的 form factor，所以没有强行映射到 PCIe 或 SXM canonical。

B200 当前为询价，也没有为了填表生成静态价格。

## L4 为什么能进入 Compare

JarvisLabs 的 L4 页面与 VM 页面同时给出单 GPU、32 vCPU、124GB RAM、USD 小时价和按分钟计费。

这些字段满足本站固定实例 Compare 的最低条件。它和 Runpod、Google Cloud 的 L4 一起，让 L4 服务商价格比较 达到三家门槛。

这只是公开配置比较，不代表本站做过性能实测。

## Pause 后怎么收费

JarvisLabs 的实例可以 Pause 和 Resume。官方 FAQ 说明暂停后不再收 compute，但保留数据继续按存储计费。

当前存储公开价是 USD 0.10/GB-month。官方 FAQ 还给出按小时折算的存储说明。

如果只是停几天，Pause 很方便。如果确定长期不用，仍应检查保留的文件系统，不要只看 GPU 已暂停。

## 适合哪些使用方式

L4 适合先做低成本推理和图像工作流。A100 80GB 适合需要较大显存但不急着用 Hopper 的任务。H100 与 H200 更适合高吞吐、大显存和多卡扩展方向。

最终要看模型是否装得下、一次任务跑多久，以及暂停后保留多少数据。小时价低，不等于整次任务一定便宜。

results.title: NVFP4 outperforms BF16 in Blackwell GPU tests
results.author: Jarvislabs.ai
highlights:
We recently tested different quantization formats for 𝗤𝘄𝗲𝗻𝟯-𝟯𝟮𝗕 on an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU. We compared BF16, FP8, MXFP8, NVFP4, and MXFP4 using vLLM.

The quality difference was small.
FP8 and MXFP8 stayed very close to BF16, while the 4-bit formats showed only a small drop in quality.

The performance difference was much more interesting.
NVFP4 reached 3,079 tokens/sec, around 𝟮.𝟰× 𝗳𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝗕𝗙𝟭𝟲.
MXFP4, even though it is also 4-bit and almost the same size, reached 1,715 tokens/sec.

We also saw a decent difference when concurrency increased.

At 360 concurrent requests:
BF16 TTFT: 8.6 sec
NVFP4 TTFT: 1.1 sec

With BF16, most of the GPU memory was already occupied by model weights, leaving less room for KV cache. As load increased, requests started spending more time in the queue.

For our setup, 𝗡𝗩𝗙𝗣𝟰 𝗴𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲.
If you want to stay as close as possible to BF16 quality, FP8 is still a solid choice.

𝗕𝘂𝘁 𝗶𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂'𝗿𝗲 𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗼𝗻 𝗕𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗸𝘄𝗲𝗹𝗹 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗺𝗼𝘀𝘁, 𝗡𝗩𝗙𝗣𝟰 𝘄𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗯𝗲 𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗽𝗶𝗰𝗸.

results.title: A lot of people assume offering GPU VMs is easy and a commodity business.
highlights:
The problem:
When we first launched GPU VMs, we ran NVIDIA's stress tests before putting servers into production. Even so, some customers ended up on GPUs with underlying issues, usually XID errors or thermal problems after a few days. That meant a bad experience for them.

What we do about it now

1. A stricter burn-in: On top of NVIDIA's stress tests, we added our own custom tests as an extra layer, and every new server runs them for more than 48 hours. If anything fails, the hardware goes back to the OEM for replacement.

2. Continuous monitoring: A GPU that passes our stress test can still become unhealthy over time, and this is the much harder problem.

We built an internal product that captures a wide range of metrics from every GPU and watches for signs of failure.

3. Automatic removal on the slightest doubt: When something looks off, the same product automatically moves the server out of production into the stress test pool, where the testing runs on its own. No one has to spot it and pull it manually.

...

This is just phase 1. The question we're working on now is whether we can use those metrics to predict a failure before it happens.

Keeping spare capacity: To replace a bad GPU quickly, you need enough healthy capacity ready to swap in.

That's expensive, because nobody likes idle GPUs. But without it, catching a problem doesn't help the customer much.

Because of all this, our customers get healthy GPUs the vast majority of the time.

What this taught us:

Price per hour is the easiest number to compare, but it leaves out most of what decides whether your workload actually runs well.

Power, cooling and rack space are only the starting point. The harder part is everything that happens after the GPUs are installed.

If you're evaluating providers for bare metal or VMs, a few questions are worth asking:

- What testing does a GPU go through before it's handed to you?
- How do they detect a GPU that degrades after it's been in production?
- How quickly can they replace a faulty GPU, and do they keep capacity for it?

A cheaper GPU that fails halfway through a training run, or takes your inference service down, usually ends up costing far more than the difference in hourly rate.

highlights:

The NVIDIA B200 is a Blackwell data center GPU with 180 GB of HBM3e at 8 TB/s per GPU, fifth-generation NVLink at 1.8 TB/s, and hardware FP4. An eight-GPU DGX B200 holds 1,440 GB of GPU memory and delivers 72 PFLOPS of dense FP4. Renting one B200 costs $5.98 to $7.99 per GPU-hour on October 24, 2026 (RunPod, Modal, Lambda), about 1.4x an H200, and NVIDIA publishes no list price for a single card. Per TB/s of memory bandwidth, the number that sets LLM decode speed, the B200 rents for less than the H200 or H100.

## NVIDIA B200 Price: Cloud Rental per GPU-Hour (October 2026)

These are the published on-demand prices for one B200, read from each provider's pricing page on October 24, 2026. Modal bills per second and charges CPU and RAM separately; RunPod and Lambda bundle host CPU, RAM, and disk into the hourly rate. Since our October 6 read, RunPod raised its Secure Cloud B200 from $6.79 to $7.99 and Lambda cut its 8x instance from $6.79 to $6.69.

B200 price per GPU-hour by provider (October 24, 2026)

| Provider | Plan | Price per GPU-hour | What is included |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Modal | Serverless, per second ($0.001736/s) | $6.25 | GPU only |
| RunPod | Community Cloud B200 pod, 180 GB | $5.98 | 180 GB VRAM, community-hosted |
| RunPod | Secure Cloud B200 pod, 180 GB | $7.99 | 28 vCPU, 283 GB RAM |
| Lambda | 8x B200 SXM6 instance | $6.69 | 208 vCPU, 2,900 GiB RAM, 22 TiB SSD |

| Morph | Dedicated inference endpoint | $9.98 | Served model, OpenAI-compatible API |

To buy, NVIDIA does not list a price for a single B200. Northflank reported OEM quotes of $45,000 to $50,000 per GPU and complete 8x B200 servers above $500,000 in August 2025. At Lambda's $6.69 per hour, $45,000 buys about 6,700 GPU-hours of rental, or nine months of one GPU running around the clock, before power, cooling, and the host server. Running one B200 all day costs $150 on Modal and $192 on RunPod Secure Cloud.

## B200 vs H200 vs H100

The H200 and H100 share Hopper compute and differ in memory. The B200 moves to Blackwell, adds FP4, and raises memory and bandwidth again. For more on the Hopper pair, see H100 vs H200 and the NVIDIA H200 guide.

results.title: AI compute crunch deepens as chip rental costs jump 60% and rivals scramble for power
results.author: Eamonn Sheridan
highlights:
- A desperate scramble for AI computing power is upending Silicon Valley, the WSJ reports, with chip rental costs up 60% in a year, rivals forced into unlikely alliances and startups squeezed by multiyear contracts and upfront fees of up to 30%.

The squeeze hands pricing power to anyone who already controls chips, data centres and electricity, favouring hyperscalers, neoclouds and chipmakers over the startups trying to rent from them. Rising rental prices and tougher contract terms point to stronger near-term revenue for compute providers, but also to growing concentration risk, as only the biggest and best-funded labs can lock in capacity. The rush to overbook capacity as a hedge raises the danger of a sharp reversal if demand disappoints, leaving firms stuck with costly lease commitments and a glut of resold capacity. That fragility echoes recent warnings that financing, power and data centre delays, not demand, are now the binding constraints on the AI build-out.

...

- A shortage of computing power is driving a frantic, industry-wide scramble across Silicon Valley, with power struggles inside companies and unlikely alliances between rivals, the Wall Street Journal (gated) reported
- The cost of renting Nvidia H100 chips on a one-year contract has risen 60% in the past year, according to research firm SemiAnalysis
- Cloud providers now demand multiyear contracts with upfront payments often as high as 30%, sometimes backed by guarantors, shutting out many smaller players
- Top executives are personally brokering deals, including Anthropic’s agreement to lease more than 300 megawatts from SpaceX, reported to be worth up to $45 billion
- Announced capacity often fails to materialise, with projects delayed, cancelled or scaled back, and some deals collapsing when data centres slip
- Venture firms are now reserving GPU clusters for their portfolio companies, as access to compute rivals capital as the key constraint for startups

...

Compute, the industry’s shorthand for computing power, has become the AI boom’s most coveted resource, and there is not enough of it. The squeeze is showing up in prices. The hourly cost of renting computing power from Nvidia’s H100 chips on a one-year contract has jumped 60% in the past year, according to research firm SemiAnalysis. Alphabet expects capital spending of up to $200 billion this year, much of it on AI infrastructure.

...

For smaller players, the terms are becoming punishing. Where startups could once rent chips flexibly, cloud providers now require multiyear contracts with upfront payments often as high as 30%, sometimes backed by guarantors. Some are turning in desperation to providers with weaker security or infrastructure. Much of the capacity that has been promised is not yet available, with projects delayed, cancelled or scaled back. One open-source startup lost a capacity deal when its partner’s data centre was delayed.

The stakes are high either way. Firms that buy too much capacity risk crippling lease commitments, while those that buy too little risk stalling their growth. Some venture capital firms are now reserving GPU clusters themselves or guaranteeing contracts on behalf of their startups.

results.title: Make Wan 2.2 render about 24% faster in ComfyUI
results.author: Sanchit Jain
highlights:
In ComfyUI's Wan 2.2 text-to-video template, set the second sampler's cfg to 1.0 and leave the first alone. Each clip renders about 24% faster, with near-identical video. A sampler is the node that runs a model; its cfg value is how strongly the model is pushed toward your prompt.

On one NVIDIA H200, with the template as it ships on Jarvislabs, a 5-second 1280×720 clip went from 632 to 477 seconds. That is about 2.5 minutes back on every clip, or 4.3 hours over 100 clips.

...

The saving comes from running the model 10 fewer times, so the share saved should be similar on any GPU that fits the models. That excludes offloading, moving parts of a model to system memory while it runs. The quality result is against the fp8 default, not full-precision weights.

results.title: How a ComfyUI Workflow Works, and How to Run It From ...
results.author: Sanchit Jain
highlights:
The models. A workflow stores the names of the models it needs, not the models. Open the template on a fresh machine and ComfyUI lists what is missing before it will run anything.

Five files, 42.97 GB, most of it one 29 GB checkpoint. They land on your volume, so you pay this once.

On a Jarvislabs instance much of this is already cached, so there is nothing to download. In future that store will hold over a hundred models.

| File | Size | What it is for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ltx-2.3-22b-dev-fp8` | 29.15 GB | The main model. Turns noise into a picture and a soundtrack. |
| `gemma_3_12B_it_fp4_mixed` | 9.45 GB | Reads your prompt and turns it into something the model understands. |
| `ltx_2.3_22b_distilled_1.1_lora` | 2.74 GB | Makes it fast. Seconds instead of minutes. |
| `ltx-2.3-spatial-upscaler-x2-1.1` | 1.00 GB | Generates at half size and doubles it, which is cheaper than making it big from the start. |
| `gemma-3-12b-it-abliterated_lora` | 0.63 GB | Adjusts how the prompt is read. We did not test what it changes. |

Every node here ships with ComfyUI — no custom packs, nothing to install. The models are the opposite: downloaded once, then kept on your volume.

> Download lands on the GPU, not your browser. ComfyUI's missing-models dialog is an ordinary browser link, so on a rented machine it fetches tens of gigabytes to the wrong computer. On a Jarvislabs instance that fetch happens on the server instead.

...

With the models already loaded, each video takes 14.38 seconds — about 1.6 cents at the H200 rate at Jarvislabs.

This is what came out of it: one photograph in, five seconds of video out.

The still we started from, and the five seconds it became. Play it with sound: the rain was generated in the same pass as the picture, from the same sentence. Nothing here was filmed or recorded.

There is no separate audio model and no separate audio step. The same model builds the picture and the sound together, in one pass, from the same sentence.

results.title: How Rising GPU Costs Are Changing Cloud Budgets for Startup Founders – foundfounders.com
results.author: Steve
highlights:
Rising GPU costs are forcing startup founders to shrink training ambitions, shift workloads to cheaper providers, and rebuild cloud budgets around compute as the single biggest line item rather than an afterthought. GPUs—the specialized chips that power AI model training and inference—have gone from a line in the infrastructure budget to the variable that decides how long a startup's runway actually lasts. The price pressure is coming from multiple directions at once: major cloud providers raising list prices, spot markets spiking on scarce supply, and hyperscalers locking up allocations before smaller buyers can get to them. Founders who built financial models around last year's GPU rates are now finding those numbers obsolete, often mid-fundraise.

...

## Why GPU Prices Jumped So Much in 2026

CoreWeave, one of the largest dedicated GPU cloud providers, raised prices by roughly 20% in late 2025 and began pushing customers toward longer commitments. It then disclosed on its Q2 2026 earnings call a further roughly 25% increase across its product lineup, implemented in July 2026. That is a compounding increase of close to 50% within a single year for customers who stayed on the same provider. Hyperscalers moved in the same direction.

AWS raised prices on its reserved EC2 Capacity Blocks—contracts that guarantee access to Nvidia H200 chips—by about 15% in early January 2026, citing supply and demand patterns. That increase came just months after AWS had cut other on-demand GPU instance prices by as much as 45%, meaning the direction of pricing now depends heavily on which specific product a startup is buying, not just which provider. Spot markets moved even faster. The Ornn Compute Price Index tracked Nvidia Blackwell GPU rental rates jumping 48% in two months, from $2.75 to $4.08 per hour by mid-April 2026. Bank of America projected at the time that GPU demand would continue outstripping supply through 2029, which signals this is not a short-term spike founders can simply wait out.

...

Specialized "neocloud" providers—smaller GPU-focused clouds like RunPod and GMI Cloud, as distinct from AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud—advertise on-demand H100 and H200 rates around $2 to $3.50 per GPU-hour in 2026. That compares with bundled hyperscaler rates of $6 to $12 or more per GPU-hour for the same chips on AWS and Azure.

...

Microsoft and other hyperscalers have been stockpiling Nvidia GPU allocations for their own cloud customers, which has squeezed the capacity available even to well-capitalized AI startups; Microsoft staff reportedly expect wait times for cloud GPU customers to persist through the end of 2026.

...

### Is the GPU price increase limited to one provider?

No. CoreWeave, AWS, and spot-market providers have all raised prices at different points in 2026, though AWS also cut some on-demand GPU rates even as it raised reserved Capacity Block prices.

results.title: A lot of people assume offering GPU VMs is easy and a commodity business. | Vishnu Subramanian
results.author: Vishnu Subramanian
highlights:
In practice, offering VMs that stay reliable over long periods is a serious engineering and operational challenge.

Here's one example from our experience at Jarvislabs.

The problem:
When we first launched GPU VMs, we ran NVIDIA's stress tests before putting servers into production. Even so, some customers ended up on GPUs with underlying issues, usually XID errors or thermal problems after a few days. That meant a bad experience for them.

What we do about it now

1. A stricter burn-in: On top of NVIDIA's stress tests, we added our own custom tests as an extra layer, and every new server runs them for more than 48 hours. If anything fails, the hardware goes back to the OEM for replacement.

2. Continuous monitoring: A GPU that passes our stress test can still become unhealthy over time, and this is the much harder problem.

We built an internal product that captures a wide range of metrics from every GPU and watches for signs of failure.

3. Automatic removal on the slightest doubt: When something looks off, the same product automatically moves the server out of production into the stress test pool, where the testing runs on its own. No one has to spot it and pull it manually.

What's next

This is just phase 1. The question we're working on now is whether we can use those metrics to predict a failure before it happens.

Keeping spare capacity: To replace a bad GPU quickly, you need enough healthy capacity ready to swap in.

That's expensive, because nobody likes idle GPUs. But without it, catching a problem doesn't help the customer much.

Because of all this, our customers get healthy GPUs the vast majority of the time.

What this taught us:

Price per hour is the easiest number to compare, but it leaves out most of what decides whether your workload actually runs well.

Power, cooling and rack space are only the starting point. The harder part is everything that happens after the GPUs are installed.

If you're evaluating providers for bare metal or VMs, a few questions are worth asking:

- What testing does a GPU go through before it's handed to you?
- How do they detect a GPU that degrades after it's been in production?
- How quickly can they replace a faulty GPU, and do they keep capacity for it?

A cheaper GPU that fails halfway through a training run, or takes your inference service down, usually ends up costing far more than the difference in hourly rate.

results.title: Lambda Labs Competitors Compared Across the GPU ...
results.author: NoraLin
highlights:
Five categories surround Lambda: enterprise-scale GPU clouds (CoreWeave) pressing with distributed infrastructure and enterprise programs; low-cost marketplaces (Vast.ai, TensorDock, Thunder Compute, Jarvislabs) pressing on per-hour price; serverless platforms (RunPod, Baseten, Modal) pressing on deployment speed for inference; energy-backed entrants (Crusoe, Fluidstack) pressing with power economics; and private dedicated enclaves (the category OneSource Cloud delivers) pressing with physical exclusivity and flat-rate predictability. Lambda sits as the AI-native simplicity player for ML teams — strongest in developer experience, exposed wherever workloads need guarantees or rock-bottom price.

...

| Category | Illustrative Names | Flagship Pressure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Enterprise-scale GPU clouds | CoreWeave | Distributed infrastructure and enterprise programs |
| Low-cost marketplaces | Vast.ai, TensorDock, Thunder, Jarvislabs | Per-hour price for fault-tolerant work |
| Serverless platforms | RunPod, Baseten, Modal | Deployment speed for inference and burst |
| Energy-backed entrants | Crusoe, Fluidstack | Power economics behind capacity claims |
| Private dedicated enclaves | OneSource Cloud | Physical exclusivity and flat-rate predictability |

...

Enterprise-scale GPU clouds (CoreWeave) press with distributed infrastructure and enterprise programs; low-cost marketplaces (Vast.ai, TensorDock, Thunder Compute, Jarvislabs) press on per-hour price for fault-tolerant work; serverless platforms (RunPod, Baseten, Modal) press on deployment speed for inference and bursty jobs; energy-backed entrants (Crusoe, Fluidstack) press with power economics behind capacity claims; and private dedicated enclaves — the category OneSource Cloud delivers with single-tenant bare metal and flat-rate pricing — press with exclusivity and cost predictability for steady regulated production. Lambda sits as the AI-native simplicity player for ML teams, strongest in developer experience and strongest in the middle of these pressures.

...

Lambda's middle position is a real strength — the simplicity pitch for ML teams lands because the product is genuinely easy to start on — but middle positions absorb pressure from both flanks. On the price flank, marketplaces undercut per-hour rates for work that tolerates variance. On the guarantee flank, the private category — OneSource Cloud as the delivered example, with single-tenant bare-metal enclaves in U.S. data centers, flat-rate monthly pricing, and zero egress fees — converts every compliance review and every unpredictable bill into a switching moment.
